newsitem.title: UK: UK's Centrica meeting heartens analysts.
newsitem.headline: UK's Centrica meeting heartens analysts.

text.p: Centrica, the trading arm of British Gas which will be spun-off via a demerger next month, impressed analysts on Tuesday with a clear outlining of strategy and positive comments on take-or-pay contract talks. "It was a very good, clear and coherent presentation on its business and how they want to go forward," said one analyst after returning from a introductory meeting with Centrica.
The meeting comes ahead of Friday's release of Centrica's listing particulars and was therefore short on details.
But Centrica did say it hoped its crippling take-or-pay problem would be solved by the end of the year, analysts said.
"Take-or-pay' contracts oblige British gas to buy gas from North Sea producers even if it cannot find a market to sell it on.
Centrica also revealed that its service and retail business would remain in deficit for longer than envisaged because it was reluctant to raise service charges.
"They previously hoped they might break-even by the end of last year. Talk now is that it will be 1998 before they're into profit," said another analyst.
"This is a bit disappointing, but it is rather more than offset by the happier news on the take-or-pay gas contract side," he added.
British Gas shares ignored these positive comments and fell 4-1/2 pence to 220-1/2, having been boosted by high hopes for today's meeting, this analyst said.

Centrica is expected to release detailed pro-forma results over the past three years on Friday. But analysts, who already know that the company will be largely debt-free, are unconvinced Centrica will come up with meaningful forecasts.

"There are a lot of areas where they genuinely cannot help us," said the first analyst at a major brokerage, referring to uncertainties over the on-going renegotiations of take-or-pay contracts and the opening up of the domestic gas market.
British Gas said last month that three contracts had already been renegotiated -- about 20 percent of the problem .

The domestic market will be completely liberalised by 1998 after a pilot project in south west of England started last year. The south east -- the second phase of the pilot -- will see the introduction of competition in the next few months.
In the loss-making industrial and commercial gas market, which was opened up in the the early 1990's, former monopolist British Gas' market share dropped to about 35 percent.
It has retained a large share in the south west so far and industry watchers reckon Centrica should be able to retain 60 to 70 percent of the domestic market in the next couple of years.
But it may well fall below 50 percent if big players such as British Petroleum step in, they warned.
Analysts were impressed nevertheless by Centrica's strategy outline today in its bid to defend itself against rivals.

"They are going to be essentially a customer service-driven organisation, so they can avoid price competition and focus on delivering good service, which is the best way to keep customers loyal," said one analyst.
Centrica will have British Gas executive Roy Gardner as its chief executive, while newspapers speculate that Sir Michael Perry, the former Unilever boss, will become chairman.

Referring to Centrica's management team, an analyst said: "They are a good group of people They know their business well and they support each other well. It is all somewhat subjective but that is all we have to go on for the moment."
-- Hans de Jongh, London Newsroom +44 171 542 7717
